proposal.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement has no indemnification section at all — Section 20 is missing even though Section 9.3 relies on "the remedies required by Section 20.5" and Section 21.3 treats indemnification obligations as Excluded Claims. We have inserted our standard Vendor indemnity (third-party IP infringement, breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused compromise of Customer Data, and gross negligence or wilful misconduct), with a reciprocal but narrow Customer indemnity limited to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law, plus customary procedure, exclusions and infringement remedies.

ops.text: Vendor shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, liabilities, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) finally awarded or paid in settlement, to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services, Deliverables, or Vendor Technology infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; (c) any unauthorized access to, acquisition, or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor or its personnel, Affiliates, or subcontractors; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct.

Customer shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Vendor from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) finally awarded or paid in settlement, to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that content or materials furnished by Customer to Vendor for use in the Services infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; or (b) Customer's breach of Applicable Law. Customer has no other indemnification obligation under this Agreement.

The indemnified Party shall give the indemnifying Party prompt written notice of the claim, provided that delay relieves the indemnifying Party only to the extent it is materially prejudiced. The indemnifying Party controls the defence and settlement with counsel reasonably acceptable to the indemnified Party, and the indemnified Party shall provide reasonable cooperation at the indemnifying Party's expense and may participate with its own counsel at its own expense. The indemnifying Party shall not settle a claim in a way that imposes a non-monetary obligation, admission of liability, or unreimbursed payment on the indemnified Party without its prior written consent.

Vendor's obligation under Section 20.1(a) does not apply to the extent the claim arises from Customer's modification of the Services or a Deliverable other than as authorized by Vendor or the documentation, combination of the Services or a Deliverable with items not supplied or recommended by Vendor where the claim would have been avoided but for the combination, or Vendor's compliance with written specifications supplied by Customer that Vendor did not select or recommend.

If a claim under Section 20.1(a) is made or Vendor reasonably believes one is likely, Vendor shall, at its expense and at Customer's option, procure the right for Customer to continue using the affected item or modify or replace it with a functionally equivalent, non-infringing item that continues to satisfy this Agreement and the applicable Order Form. If Vendor cannot do so on commercially reasonable terms, Customer may terminate the affected Services, Deliverables, or Order Form and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees for the terminated portion and, for a paid-up licence, the Fees paid for the affected item.

rationale: The Agreement contains no indemnification provision. The outline jumps from Section 19 (Warranties) straight to Section 21 (Limitation of Liability), so Section 20 is absent entirely: there is no Vendor defence/indemnity for third-party IP infringement, breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused data compromise, or gross negligence/wilful misconduct, and no indemnification procedure. Other clauses assume the section exists — Section 9.3 conditions Customer's termination right on Vendor's inability to "provide the remedies required by Section 20.5", Section 19.4 preserves remedies for "indemnified claims", Section 21.3 makes "its indemnification obligations" an Excluded Claim, and Section 30.5 refers to an "indemnified party" and "vested indemnity rights" — leaving dangling cross-references. This is a critical gap approaching the walk-away position (no Vendor IP indemnity at all). We therefore insert a new Section 20 after Section 19.5 implementing the preferred position: Vendor defends and indemnifies Customer and its Affiliates for IP infringement, breach of law, Vendor-caused unauthorized access to Customer Data, and gross negligence/wilful misconduct; a narrow Customer indemnity limited to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law; standard notice/control/cooperation procedure; customary IP exclusions; and Section 20.5 procure/modify/replace/refund remedies, which also repairs the Section 9.3 cross-reference. No liability super-cap is needed because Section 21.3 already carves indemnification obligations out of the cap.

quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: Section 21.1 imposes a mutual cap at the greater of Fees paid or payable by Customer in the 12 months preceding the event and USD 1,000,000, exactly the preferred basis. Section 21.2 excludes indirect/consequential damages mutually and confirms data restoration, replacement services, breach notification and incident response costs are direct damages. Section 21.3 defines "Excluded Claims" to cover confidentiality, data-protection and security breaches, indemnification obligations, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and infringement of the other Party's IP; because both 21.1 and 21.2 open "Except for Excluded Claims," those carve-outs sit outside the cap and are uncapped rather than merely excluded. Section 21.3 also confirms Customer's obligation to pay undisputed Fees is not "damages" and is not limited. "Fees" (§1.5) covers recurring subscription, professional services and usage fees, so with the §2.1 commitment of USD 2,000,000 per year the 12-month fee basis is meaningful, not illusory. Section 21.4 preserves unlimited liability where it cannot lawfully be limited and makes each cap independent of failure of an exclusive remedy; §18.2 confirms insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities, and no competing cap or one-sided "aggregate liability" language appears in the warranty, indemnity or insurance provisions. No redline needed.

quote: 22.1 Vendor may audit Customer's compliance with licence quantities no more than once in any twelve-month period, on at least thirty days' prior written notice, during normal business hours, and in a manner that does not unreasonably disrupt Customer. An audit will be conducted off-site where practicable by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality.
rationale: Section 22 meets every element of the preferred position: audits are limited to once per twelve-month period (22.1), require thirty days' prior written notice during normal business hours (22.1), are conducted off-site where practicable by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality (22.1), are at Vendor's cost unless the audit establishes underpayment exceeding five percent (22.2), and expressly bar Vendor and its auditor from accessing Customer systems directly or unrelated Customer Data, privileged material, or other suppliers' confidential information (22.2). Section 22.3 adds Customer-favourable protections (findings are Customer Confidential Information, use limited to enforcement, copy of final report, payment resolves the issue). Section 23 (Records and Customer Assurance) contains only a heading with no substantive paragraphs, so it creates no broader audit or inspection path against Customer, and no other clause in the Agreement grants Vendor inspection, verification, or monitoring rights over Customer. No redline is required.
sectionRef: § 22.1 Vendor may audit Customer's compliance with licence quantit…

verification.notes: Cited text (22.1–22.2) satisfies every element of the preferred position: one audit per twelve-month period, thirty days' prior written notice, normal business hours, off-site where practicable by an independent auditor bound by confidentiality, Vendor bears cost unless underpayment exceeds five percent, and an express bar on direct access to Customer systems and unrelated Customer Data. Section 22.3 adds Customer-favourable protections (findings treated as Customer Confidential Information, use limited to enforcement, copy of final report, payment resolves the issue), so no residual gap exists. Consistent with a compliant finding, no redline or counterparty comment was proposed and the paragraphs are returned unchanged; the deterministic frequency check also passes.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 10 winds down access and Deliverables but says nothing about exit support or getting our data back, so we have added a transition-assistance and data-return provision: up to six months' assistance at Vendor's then-current rates, return of Customer Data in a machine-readable format within thirty days, and certified deletion thereafter. If six months is an issue we can accept ninety days of assistance, provided the thirty-day export and deletion certification remain.

ops.text: 10.3 Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement or any Order Form for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty days of Customer's request, return or make available for download all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems, subject to routine backups and legal retention requirements, and certify such deletion in writing.

quote: 10.2 Vendor shall deliver all completed and in-process Deliverables for which Customer has paid or agrees to pay the applicable proportionate Fees. Vendor shall refund prepaid recurring Fees covering the period after termination, together with Fees paid for Services Customer cannot reasonably use because of Vendor's uncured breach.
rationale: Section 10 (Effect of Expiry or Termination) addresses only access wind-down (10.1) and Deliverable delivery plus refunds (10.2). There is no transition-assistance period, no obligation to return or export Customer Data in a machine-readable format, and no deletion or deletion-certification obligation; searches for "transition assistance", "export" and "delete" return nothing relevant, and Section 16.5 expressly carves Customer Data out to "Sections 11 and 15" while Section 11 does not exist in the document. Section 15 covers processing limits only. In a hosted services agreement this absence is a deviation, so we insert a new Section 10.3 with six months of transition assistance at Vendor's then-current rates, return of Customer Data within thirty days, and certified deletion thereafter.

verification.notes: The inserted Section 10.3 sits correctly at the end of the termination-effects section (after 10.2) and tracks the preferred position: up to six months' transition assistance at Vendor's then-current rates, return of Customer Data in a commonly used machine-readable format within thirty days, and certified deletion thereafter. The edit is purely additive — the existing text of p0042 is untouched — which is the smallest edit capable of curing a 'missing' provision. The comment accurately describes the gap (Section 10 covers only access wind-down and Deliverables), states what was added, and offers the playbook fallback (90 days) while preserving the 30-day export and deletion certification; tone and prefix conform. Minor drafting deltas ('within thirty days of Customer's request'; deletion 'subject to routine backups and legal retention requirements') are commercially standard qualifiers that do not fall to the walk-away line (no data return or immediate deletion), so they do not defeat the rule; flag only if the reviewer wants the 30-day clock to run automatically from termination.

quote: 19.2 For ninety days after delivery or acceptance, whichever is later, each Deliverable will materially conform to its documentation and acceptance criteria. Hosted Services will conform throughout the subscription term.
rationale: Section 19 meets or exceeds the preferred WARRANTY position, so no redline is warranted. §19.1 gives a professional and workmanlike standard performed by qualified personnel to industry standards, plus an untimed warranty that Services and Deliverables will materially conform to documentation and specifications. §19.2 gives 90 days after the later of delivery or acceptance for each Deliverable — and because "Deliverable" under §1.4 is bespoke work product (reports, configurations, integrations, training material) rather than licensed software, 90 days matches our preferred services-side period; the software/hosted element is warranted to conform throughout the whole subscription term, exceeding our 12-month preferred software period. §19.3 adds compliance with Applicable Law, a no-malicious-code warranty, and no-functionality-diminution and open-source protections. §19.4 delivers the full preferred remedy stack: prompt re-performance, repair or replacement at no charge, escalating to termination of the affected item and refund of Fees paid if Vendor cannot cure within a reasonable period, and expressly non-exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims; §6.2 adds acceptance-stage correction and refund rights. §19.5 confirms the disclaimer is mutual, limited to implied warranties, and does not limit any express warranty, service level, indemnity, confidentiality or data-protection duty, so the disclaimer does not swallow the express warranty. The only softening is that the malicious-code warranty is limited to code "intentionally introduced by Vendor," which is market-standard and does not undercut the position given the non-exclusive remedies; it is not worth reopening a favourable package. The spelled-out "ninety days" phrasing is legally unambiguous and is a drafting-convention point only, not a substantive shortfall.
